# ct25519 — SPEC

## Maturity

**Grade:** 2 · S2 E2 A2 H1 P1 · limited by scope (parity), evidence (EXTERNAL, frozen vectors only -- no tools/interop.zig), audit (src changed since) *(generated by `zig build gen-catalog`)*

Scalar multiplication on Edwards25519 / Ristretto255 that is safe to hand a
**secret** scalar; see [README.md](README.md) for purpose and API.
Provenance: clean-room re-derivation of the fixed-window ladder in Zig's own
`std/crypto/25519/edwards25519.zig` — see the `Provenance:` line in
[README.md](README.md) and the module's [`NOTICE`](NOTICE) (the one ported OpenSSL squaring and the ladder-step order). The benchmark driver `tools/c_bench/foreign_bench.c` is generated by our own
tooling (our own code running libsodium and OpenSSL as black-box oracles for timing).

**Where we are ahead:** the only pure-Zig secret-scalar Edwards/Ristretto multiplication with no error path; comb base-point multiplication 2.6× `std`'s ladder; X25519 key generation 2.36× and an x86-64 MULX/ADX shared-secret ladder faster than `std`'s (the card's Performance line carries the ratios against libsodium and OpenSSL); ctgrind-checked with positive controls; scalar wiped from the callee's frame; a Straus multi-scalar for Ristretto. **Secret-scalar surface against dalek's, item by item:** `EdwardsPoint * Scalar` = `mul`; `EdwardsPoint::mul_base` = `mulBase` (comb, as dalek's table); `RistrettoPoint * Scalar` / `mul_base` = `mulRistretto` / `mulRistrettoBase`; `MontgomeryPoint * Scalar`, `mul_clamped`, `mul_base_clamped` = `X25519.scalarmult` / `recoverPublicKey` (clamping per RFC 7748); constant-time `MultiscalarMul` on Ristretto = `mulMultiRistretto` and on Edwards = `mulMulti`; `Scalar::invert` = std's `scalar.Scalar.invert` (a fixed addition chain, constant-time). Every one present. **Where we are behind, and why it is not a gap a user hits:** `Scalar::batch_invert` (a speed-up over n `invert` calls, not a missing operation); `EdwardsBasepointTable::create` for a caller's own fixed point (a speed-up for repeated `mul` by the same point; `mul` gives the same result); variable-time MSM, hash-to-curve, Elligator and the point types themselves (public-data operations `std` provides — outside this module's secret-scalar scope by design); no vectorised (AVX2/AVX-512) backend and no arm64 field core (speed on other hardware: P axis and Backlog).

## Design

- **Source of truth**: `std.crypto.ecc.Edwards25519`'s own constant-time
  ladder. `mul`/`mulRistretto` are not a new algorithm and must never become
  one — they are std's `pcMul16` with exactly one thing removed. Anything else
  that diverges from std is a bug in this module, and the differential tests
  exist to say so.
  ⚠ **One documented exception:** `mulBase` and
  `mulRistrettoBase` use a fixed-base comb instead of the ladder (audit C3),
  admitted as an exception to "never a new algorithm", with the evidence in § "C3 — the base point
  uses a fixed-base comb" below. `mul(Edwards25519.basePoint, s)` is still the
  ladder, and it is the comb's reference.
- **std recon (confirmed against `lib/std/crypto/25519/edwards25519.zig`,
  0.16.0)**:
  - `mul(p, s)` is `pc = if (p.is_base) basePointPc else precompute(p, 15)`
    (with `xpc[4].rejectIdentity() catch return error.WeakPublicKey`), then
    `pcMul16(&pc, s, false)`.
  - `pcMul16` is a 4-bit fixed window: `q = identity`, then 64 iterations
    from `pos = 252` down to `0` in steps of 4, each an unconditional
    `pcSelect(16, pc, slot)` + `add`, followed by four `dbl`s except on the
    last. `pcSelect` is branch-free: `t = identity`, then a `cMov` of every
    entry `1..15` under the mask `((slot ^ i) -% 1) >> 8) & 1`.
  - `pcMul16` **ends with `try q.rejectIdentity()`** (`:266`). That single
    line is the entire reason this module exists: `rejectIdentity` is
    `if (p.x.isZero())`, a branch on a value derived from the scalar, and
    the error union it forces makes the branch contagious — every caller
    has to branch a second time to handle `error.IdentityElement`.
  - `precompute(p, 15)` builds `pc[i] = i·p` by `pc[i/2].dbl()` for even `i`
    and `pc[i-1].add(p)` for odd; `basePointPc` folds it at comptime.
  - `Ristretto255.mul` is `.{ .p = try p.p.mul(s) }` — a thin wrapper, so it
    inherits the rejection unchanged. `Ristretto255.basePoint` is
    `.{ .p = Curve.basePoint }`, so its `is_base` flag is set and the
    comptime table is reached through it.
- **What this module changes**: the trailing `rejectIdentity` is gone and
  the input-point `WeakPublicKey` check is gone. Nothing else. `precompute`
  and `pcSelect` are transcriptions of std's private versions (std does not
  export them), and `base_pc` is the same comptime fold. Same table, same 64
  iterations, same cost.
- **`pc[0]` is dead by construction.** `precompute` writes
  `pc[0] = identityElement` and `pcSelect` starts its `cMov` chain at `i = 1`
  (returning the identity when `slot == 0`), so index 0 is never read. It is
  kept for shape-parity with std. A fault injected into `pc[0]` is green
  because the code is dead, not because the tests are weak — noted here so a
  future auditor does not re-derive that the hard way.
- **All 256 scalar bits are consumed.** The top window at `pos = 252` covers
  bits 252..255, so `mul(P, s)` is `s·P` for the full 256-bit integer `s`,
  not for `s mod L`. A caller that needs the reduced value reduces first
  (`scalar.reduce`/`reduce64`), exactly as it must for std.

## C3 — the base point uses a fixed-base comb (an exception to "never a new algorithm")

**Why.** `mulBase` was `mul(basePoint, s)`: 64 window additions and **252
doublings** over a 16-entry table, 71 % of its time in the doublings, 2.81×
libsodium's base multiply (audit C3, 52.5 vs 18.7 µs). Five modules pay it —
`ecvrf` (`publicKey`, the nonce commitment `k·B`), `signal` (XEdDSA key point
and nonce), `voprf` (`skS·B`, POPRF tweak), `opaque` through `voprf`.

**Technique and source.** The fixed-base comb of Bernstein, Duif, Lange,
Schwabe, Yang, "High-speed high-security signatures" (J. Cryptogr. Eng. 2012)
§4, i.e. ref10's `ge_scalarmult_base` and libsodium's
`ge25519_scalarmult_base`, implemented from that description:

- `s` is recoded into signed radix-16 digits `e[0..64]` in `[-8, 7]`
  (`combRecode`: `x = nibble + carry`, `carry = (x + 8) >> 4`,
  `e = x − 16·carry`), so `s = Σ e[i]·16^i + carry·16^64`;
- `comb_table[j][k] = (k+1)·16^(2j)·B`, 32×8 points in extended coordinates,
  folded at comptime from std's `add`/`dbl` (~480 operations);
- `q = Σ_{i odd} e[i]·16^(i−1)·B`, four doublings, then `+ Σ_{i even}
  e[i]·16^i·B`: **64 additions and 4 doublings**.
- ⚠ **Deviation from ref10, deliberate.** ref10 requires `s[31] ≤ 127` so its
  top digit can absorb the carry. This module reads all 256 bits (the `mul`
  contract), so the carry out of digit 63 stays a secret bit and one extra,
  always-performed add selects `2^256·B` (`comb_carry`) or the identity by
  `cMov`.

Constant-time shape: 64 digit iterations whatever `s` is; recoding by
shift/mask; each row gathered by a full 8-entry `cMov` scan (the `pcSelect`
mask) and the sign by `cMov` onto `−x`/`−t`; table indices are loop counters.
That is the design, not the evidence — evidence 3 is.
**Dispatch.** `mulBase`, `mulRistrettoBase` and `X25519.recoverPublicKey` go through `baseMul` (`src/root.zig:350`): the 4×64 comb of § P8 where the build has BMI2 and the LLVM backend (`fast_ed`, `root.zig:1368`), this portable 4-bit comb (`combMulBase`, `root.zig:298`) elsewhere, and `mul`'s window ladder over `base_pc` when the `ct25519-base-comb` option is off (§ Build options).

**Evidence** (all in-tree):

1. **Bit-exact against the previous implementation.** The reference is `mul(Edwards25519.basePoint, s)` / `mulRistretto(Ristretto255.basePoint, s)` — byte for byte the pre-comb `mulBase` / `mulRistrettoBase` — compared on the canonical encoding, both groups: every nibble value 0..15 at every position 0..63 (reaches all 256 table entries with both signs, every carry, and the carry point); boundary and carry-chain scalars (`0`, `L−1`, `L`, `L+1`, `2L`, `2^256−L`, `2^252`, `2^255±1`, `2^256−1`, all-`0x88` where the carry ripples through all 64 digits, all-`0x77`, alternating patterns, …); the RFC 8032 §7.1 public keys (the external anchor) through the comb; the table itself entry by entry against the ladder, `comb_carry` against `16·(2^252·B)`, and the recoding against integer reconstruction with the digit range asserted (`root.zig`–`:2300`).
2. **Randomized differential** against the same reference over raw 256-bit and reduced scalars (`root.zig`); mutants of the recoding, the sign handling, the doubling count, the carry add, the row selection and the nibble order turn it red, and two correct rewrites (carry by compare, table by additions only) stay green.
3. **ctgrind targets** `comb` (`mulBase`), `ladderbase` (`mul(basePoint, s)`), `ladder` (a point decoded at run time) and `ct25519` (`mulRistrettoBase`): tainted scalar, no context in `root.zig`, the same two out-of-file witness contexts, untainted and no-`-fvalgrind` controls 0. Positive controls on the comb: a branch on the recoding carry, and a secret-indexed row read, each add in-file contexts at the mutated line while `ladderbase` and `ladder` stay at 0 (the targets localise). The measured rows are pinned in `scripts/checks/ctgrind-expected.tsv`.
4. **This section**: the comb is an exception to "never a new algorithm" because it is 2.6× faster on the one operation every secret-key derivation and every Schnorr-style nonce commitment in the consumers named above performs, with no change to the contract (constant-time, total, all 256 bits, no error union, same result on every input) and the old algorithm kept in the module as a standing oracle. The cost is the comptime-folded table (sizes in § Build options), a recoding step with no std counterpart, and one more path the ctgrind gate has to measure.

`src/bench.zig` (`CT25519_BENCH=1 scripts/modtest ct25519
-Doptimize=ReleaseFast`) re-runs the same pairs in-module (audit C9).

## B9 — constant-time multi-scalar multiplication (an exception to "never a new algorithm")

**Why.** `bulletproofs`' prover sums `Σ s_i·P_i` over SECRET witness and
blinding scalars (`A`, `S`, every IPA round's `L`/`R`). It did that as one
full `mulRistretto` per term — 252 doublings per term — and its SPEC called
that "a documented by-design boundary" because the fast bucket (Pippenger)
method branches on digits. Audit `bulletproofs` B9 measured the dilemma as
false: dalek's constant-time `MultiscalarMul` is 2.45× the per-term loop at
n = 64.

**Technique and source.** Straus's interleaving (E. G. Straus, "Addition
chains of vectors", Amer. Math. Monthly 71, 1964) with this module's own
4-bit fixed window and `pcSelect`: every term keeps its 16-entry table, and
all terms share ONE chain of doublings — per window, one `pcSelect`+add per
term, then four doublings for the group. No digit decides whether an add
happens or which bucket it lands in, which is what makes it constant-time
where Pippenger is not. Implemented from that description.
`mulMultiRistretto(scalars, points)`, and `mulMulti(scalars,
points)` on raw Edwards25519 points — the same Straus pass (`strausChunk` is
generic over the point type; a Ristretto point contributes its Edwards
representative `.p`); terms are processed in chunks of
`msm_chunk = 8` so the tables (≈ 21.5 KiB) live on the stack and no allocator
is needed. Chunking changes nothing in the result (the chunk-size mutants
below are green) and depends only on `scalars.len`, which is public. A length
mismatch panics: an error union is the shape this module refuses, and
`bulletproofs` checks the lengths before calling.
**Evidence:**

1. **Bit-exact against the loop it replaces.** The reference is the sum of `mulRistretto` products, i.e. the pre-Straus `bulletproofs.multiScalarMul`, compared on the canonical encoding at every chunk boundary (n = 0, 1, 2, 7, 8, 9, 15, 16, 17, 24, 33, 64; Debug stops at 17) with raw 256-bit, reduced and edge scalars (`0`, `1`, `L−1`, `L`, `2^256−1`, all-`0x88`) and the flagged base point, an unflagged decoded base point, the identity and random points; plus one term against `mulRistretto` for every edge scalar and zero terms against the identity (`root.zig`, `:2384`). `mulMulti` on Edwards points is held to the per-term `mul` sum with torsion components added (orders 2 and 4 on random points), to std's variable-time `Edwards25519.mulMulti` on public data, and one term to `mul` (`root.zig`–`:2465`). `bulletproofs`' own `B9 diff` test holds its `multiScalarMul` to the verbatim pre-Straus body.
2. **Randomized differential**, the same tests, with mutants that turn them red: every term reading the first table, three shared doublings per window, the trailing partial chunk skipped, a chunk's result overwriting the running total, every term on the base-point table, the window nibble shifted one bit; doubling the Edwards input point fails all three Edwards tests. Chunk sizes 5 and 1 (the latter is the per-term ladder again) stay green, as they must.
3. **ctgrind target `msm`**: 9 terms (a full chunk plus one), every scalar derived from the tainted secret, public runtime points, running both `mulMultiRistretto` and `mulMulti`; no context in `root.zig`, controls 0. Positive control: replacing the `pcSelect` add with `if (slot != 0) q = q.add(t[slot])` puts contexts on the mutated line. In `bulletproofs`' own gate the `rangeproof` and `ipa` rows stay at 0 in-file with this MSM in the prover, and `ipa`'s pinned output digest still matches (the transcript hashes every `L`/`R`, so it is byte-identical). The stack probe covers both functions (`src/stackprobe_test.zig`).
4. **This section**: one of the two prover hot paths drops by the 2.45× the audit measured for dalek's constant-time MSM at n = 64 without giving up constant time — the property the old loop was kept for — and the primitive is ~40 lines that reuse `precompute` / `pcSelect` unchanged, held byte-exact to the loop it replaces.

## X25519 key generation on the comb

**Why.** The web-server consumer's TLS server profile (churn lane, `perf record`) had
X25519 at ~28 % of the handshake's CPU, split evenly between the ephemeral
key pair and the shared secret: `std.crypto.dh.X25519.recoverPublicKey` runs
the same 255-step Montgomery ladder over `u = 9` as `scalarmult` runs over a
peer's point. Only 1.15× behind OpenSSL's ladder, so an asm field core would
buy little; the base-point half is a fixed-base multiply, which is what C3's
comb is for.

**What.** `X25519` — `std.crypto.dh.X25519`'s declarations (`Curve`, the
four lengths, `KeyPair` with `generateDeterministic`/`generate`,
`recoverPublicKey`, `scalarmult`) — with `recoverPublicKey` as
`clamp(sk)·B` on the comb followed by the birational map to Montgomery `u`
(RFC 7748 §4.1): `u = (1 + y)/(1 − y) = (Z + Y)/(Z − Y)` in extended
coordinates, one `Fe.invert` (std's `Curve25519.fromEdwards25519` spends two).
`scalarmult` IS std's, re-exported. Clamping is std's `scalar.clamp`, so the
bytes are std's bytes.

**No identity branch.** std's `recoverPublicKey` ends in `rejectIdentity`.
Here the result is returned unconditionally: for a clamped scalar
`k ∈ [2^254, 2^255)` with `8 | k`, `k·B = O` iff `L | k`, and the multiples
of `L` in that range are `4L..7L`, none divisible by 8. The
`IdentityElementError` in the signatures is std's shape kept for drop-in use
(the web-server consumer's TLS fork binds the type by one declaration); it is never produced.
**Evidence.**
- Test `X25519: RFC 7748 §6.1's published key pairs and shared secret` re-derives Alice's and Bob's public keys byte-exactly and the shared secret both ways through `scalarmult` (`root.zig`).
- Test `X25519: recoverPublicKey is bit-exact with std over random and edge seeds`: SHA-512-derived RAW seeds (not reduced: every bit pattern is a legal secret, so bits 254/255 and the low three are exercised through the clamp) plus all-zero, all-one and single-bit edges (`root.zig`).
- Test `X25519: a key pair from the comb agrees with a std key pair on the shared secret`: mixed key pairs, and `generate(io)` has the type's shape (`root.zig`).
- ctgrind target `x25519` (`scripts/checks/ctgrind.sh ct25519`): tainted seed, no context in this module's code — the same two out-of-file contexts `comb` shows (std's `Fe.toBytes` final reduction and the harness print); untainted control 0, no-`-fvalgrind` trap 0. With the identity branch in (a first draft) there was a third context at the `isZero` compare in `recoverPublicKey`, which is why the branch is not there.
- The bench (`CT25519_BENCH=1`) times `recoverPublicKey` against std's and the comb against the ladder in the same run; the card's Performance line is authoritative for figures.

**Limits.** Only key generation changes here; the shared secret is § P6
below. A consumer that needs `KeyPair.fromEd25519`/`publicKeyFromEd25519`
takes them from std.

## P6 — X25519 shared secret on a 4×64-bit field core in MULX/ADX assembly

**Why.** The web-server consumer's TLS churn lane (after the comb took key
generation) had `X25519.scalarmult` — the shared-secret ladder over the
peer's `u` — as its largest single item, **18.65 % of CPU**. std's ladder is
RFC 7748 §5 on a 5×51-bit field with `u128` products: 25 multiplies per
field multiplication, ~1.15× behind OpenSSL's.

**Technique and sources.** GF(2^255 − 19) on four 64-bit limbs, the x86-64
representation of Oliveira, López, Hışıl, Faz-Hernández, Rodríguez-
Henríquez, "How to (pre-)compute a ladder: improving the performance of
X25519 and X448" (SAC 2017) and Nath & Sarkar, "Efficient arithmetic in
(pseudo-)Mersenne prime order fields" (IACR ePrint 2018/985), implemented
from those descriptions and the arithmetic itself:

- a value is `[4]u64` in `[0, 2^256)`, only **congruent** mod p — every
  operation maps `[0, 2^256)` into `[0, 2^256)`, so no intermediate bound
  has to be tracked; `toBytes` is the only full reduction (fold bit 255 as
  `+19`, then subtract p under a mask derived from bit 255 of `v + 19`);
- multiplication: 4×4 schoolbook, 16 `mulx`, then `t0..t3 + 38·(t4..t7)`
  (`2^256 ≡ 38`), the fifth word folded as `+38·top` and one more masked
  `+38` if that carried (a second carry is impossible: after a wrap the low
  words are below `38·2^32`); squaring: 6 cross products doubled by an add
  chain plus 4 diagonal squares, 10 `mulx`, same reduction; `add`/`sub`: a
  257-bit sum/difference, the carry/borrow folded as `±38` twice by mask;
  `·121665` (RFC 7748's `a24`): 4 `mulx` and a fold;
- the ladder is RFC 7748 §5 verbatim (`x_2 = AA·BB`,
  `z_2 = E·(AA + a24·E)`), 255 steps over bits 254..0 of the clamped scalar
  (std's `ladder(p, s, 255)` runs the same steps), the swap an xor mask
  (`cswap`), then `x_2 · z_2^(p−2)` by a fixed chain of 254 squarings and 11
  multiplications;
- all field elements of the ladder and the inversion live in ONE array and
  every operation addresses its operands as compile-time offsets from one
  base register. The first draft passed three pointers per operation; with
  the multiplication's eleven registers that compiled in Debug and failed
  in ReleaseFast ("inline assembly requires more registers than available"), where LLVM reserves a frame/base pointer.

**Dispatch (compile time, never CPUID).**

| build | `X25519.scalarmult` |
|---|---|
| x86-64, LLVM backend, target has `bmi2` and `adx` | `mulx` + two carry chains (`adcx` on CF, `adox` on OF) in the multiplication and its reduction; squaring, add/sub as below |
| x86-64, LLVM backend, `bmi2` without `adx` — e.g. The web-server consumer's `accel-amd64` = `x86_64_v3+aes+pclmul` | `mulx` with single `adc` carry chains everywhere (the row product is formed as five words first, then added; three finished product words are parked in the output slot to free registers) |
| anything else: baseline `x86_64`, other architectures, the self-hosted backend | std's `std.crypto.dh.X25519.scalarmult`, unchanged |

The asm is compiled only where the LLVM backend emits it
(`builtin.zig_backend == .stage2_llvm`, `.claude/rules/zig-pitfalls.md`),
and only with the feature in the build target — there is no run-time
detection, so a binary never executes an instruction its target does not
promise. The MULX-only path exists because the web-server consumer's deployment target has BMI2
and not ADX (x86-64-v3 does not include ADX); on this Kaby Lake it runs at
the same ratio to std as the ADX path. `test_hooks.forced` (test builds
only, empty otherwise — the `sha2` pattern) lets one test run hold every
compiled path to std.

**Constant-time argument, per instruction class.**

- *Control flow:* every asm block is straight-line; the ladder loop and the
  inversion chain run a fixed number of iterations (255, 254 + 11); the
  bit index is the loop counter.
- *Memory addresses:* the state pointer plus compile-time offsets; the only
  secret-derived index would be the swap, and it is an xor mask over both
  slots (`m = 0 − bit`, `t = m & (x ⊕ y)`), not a selection.
- *Arithmetic:* `mov`, `add`/`adc`/`sub`/`sbb`, `adcx`/`adox`, `mulx`,
  `imul` by the constant 38, `and`, `xor` — classes Intel lists as having
  data-operand-independent timing. No division, no variable shift, no
  `cmov` needed. Carry folds are `sbb r,r; and $38,r; add r,…`.
- *The one branch:* std's API returns `error.IdentityElement` for an
  all-zero shared secret, and `scalarmult` keeps that shape (drop-in for
  the web-server consumer's TLS shim, which binds the function type). The zero flag is an OR
  over the output bytes; the branch on it depends on the PUBLIC point only:
  a clamped `k = 8·m ∈ [2^254, 2^255)`, and `k·P = O` iff the order of `P`
  divides `k`. On the curve (order `8L`) the prime part `L` would need
  `L | m`, but the multiples of `L` in range are `4L..7L`, none divisible by
  8; on the twist (order `4L' = 2p + 2 − 8L`, `L' ≈ 2^253`) the multiples
  of `L'` in range are `3L'` and `4L'` (`2L'` is just below `2^254`, `4L'`
  just below `2^255`), neither divisible by 8. So
  the output is zero iff `P` has order dividing 8 (curve) or 4 (twist) — a
  property of the peer's key. The flag is therefore declassified for
  memcheck (`makeMemDefined`, a no-op without `-fvalgrind`), exactly one
  byte, so the harness keeps measuring the secret.
- *What the claim is not:* the § "Threat model / limits" boundary applies
  unchanged — a statement about the instructions and the machine code
  measured, not about any microarchitecture, and ctgrind (below) is the
  evidence, not this list.
**Evidence.**

- *External vectors, every backend:* RFC 7748 §5.2's two vectors (the second has the top bit of `u` set), the 1- and 1 000-iteration chains, §6.1's key pairs through the LADDER over `u = 9` and the shared secret both ways. The 1 000 000-iteration chain is opt-in (`CT25519_RFC7748_MILLION=1`, the build's default backend only) (`root.zig`–`:2613`).
- *Differential vs std, every asm backend:* random raw (scalar, `u`) pairs per backend (raw means the top bit of `u` is set half the time and the scalar is unclamped); and the edge `u`s 0, 1, 2, 9, 19, p−1, p, p+1, p+9, p+18, 2^255−1, 2^256−1, 2^255, limb boundaries, every Montgomery `u` of the order-2/4/8 points (mapped from an order-8 Edwards point) and their non-canonical `+p` twins, each × several scalars (incl. all-zero and all-one) × top bit of `u` clear and set; the value AND `error.IdentityElement` must agree, and the test asserts std rejects at least 6 of the edge points, so the error path is exercised (`root.zig`, `:2725`).
- *Field level vs `u512` mod p, both asm paths:* `mul`, `sq`, `add`, `sub`, `·121665`, `toBytes` over edge values × edge values (0, 1, 18, 19, 37, 38, 39, p−1, p, p+1, p+18, 2^255±1, 2p−1, 2p, 2p+1, 2^256−1, 2^256−38, 2^256−39, every limb boundary, alternating half-words) and random pairs, two thirds biased to saturated limbs so every carry chain runs its full length; the in-place forms (`o` = an input) of every op that allows them; `invert` as `z·z⁻¹ ≡ 1` and `0, p ↦ 0`. Every state slot is pre-filled with junk, so a stale answer cannot pass (`root.zig`, `:2850`).
- *ctgrind target `x25519`* (`scripts/checks/ctgrind.sh ct25519`, ReleaseFast, `-fvalgrind`, native MULX+ADX host): runs `recoverPublicKey` AND `scalarmult` of the same tainted key against RFC 7748 §6.1 Bob's key (decoded at run time) and prints both results. Tainted: no context in `root.zig`, the witnesses are the `result=` and `shared=` prints (taint reached the shared secret); untainted and no-`-fvalgrind` controls 0. The `-mcpu=x86_64_v3` (MULX-only) path is measured by hand with the same harness. Positive controls, each adding one in-file context at the mutated line: declassify removed (at `if (acc == 0)` in `sharedSecret`), and `cswap` as `if (swap != 0) swap(…)` on both the native and the MULX-only build. On a build without BMI2 the target measures std's ladder, whose own `isZero` branch the pattern does not attribute — the row would go red there, which is the right failure: it would be measuring a different path.
- *Bench:* `CT25519_BENCH=1 scripts/modtest ct25519 -Doptimize=ReleaseFast` times the new ladder against `std.crypto.dh.X25519.scalarmult` in the same process; the card's Performance line carries the figures.

## Threat model / limits

- **The claim.** `mul`/`mulBase`/`mulRistretto`/`mulRistrettoBase` execute
  the same sequence of operations for every scalar, including zero and
  including `s ≡ 0 (mod L)`, and none of them can return an error, so no
  call site can branch on the scalar either. That is the whole claim.
- **What the claim is NOT.** It is a claim about *this source* and about the
  machine code LLVM emits from it on the builds measured below. It is not a
  claim about the microarchitecture: nothing here constrains cache behaviour,
  execution-port contention, data-dependent µop latency, or speculation, and
  a `cMov` is not guaranteed by any ISA contract to be constant-time. Nor is
  it a claim that holds under an arbitrary future compiler — LLVM is free to
  rematerialise a branch out of a mask, and only a re-run of the check below
  can say whether it did. **Overclaiming this is the single most common
  defect the audit found; the honest boundary is the deliverable.**
- **Points are the caller's problem.** `mul` performs no validation of `p` —
  no identity check, no low-order check. That is deliberate (a second error
  union, over what is public data in every consumer), and it is a contract:
  where the point is attacker-supplied the caller MUST reject the identity
  and, on raw Edwards25519 (cofactor 8), low-order points, before calling.
  ristretto255 has prime order, so a decoded non-identity element is enough.
  ⚠ **Canonicity alone is not enough.** std's `rejectNonCanonical` only checks
  `y < p` and misses two signed-bit encodings that share a residue with a
  canonical one: `01…80` re-encodes the identity and `ec…ff` re-encodes
  `p−1` — both decode (via `fromBytes`) to points of low order, and both
  read `rejectNonCanonical` reports as canonical. A caller that treats
  "ran `rejectNonCanonical`" as sufficient point validation lets both
  through; `rejectLowOrder`/`rejectIdentity` is mandatory regardless of
  what `rejectNonCanonical` said. Checked against std's
  `fromBytes`/`rejectNonCanonical` on five degenerate encodings.
- **How "the shared secret MUST NOT be the identity" is discharged.** Over a
  prime-order group with a validated non-identity `P`, `s·P` is the identity
  **iff `s ≡ 0 (mod L)`** — a degenerate *local* secret, never something a
  peer can induce with any element it can encode. Protocol rules of that
  shape are therefore satisfied structurally, by validating `P` and
  generating `s` properly, and not by a runtime branch on secret-derived
  data. `opaque` (RFC 9807 §6.4.1.1) and `voprf` both rely on exactly this.
- **Public scalars belong on std.** A signature's `s`, a Fiat-Shamir
  challenge a verifier replays, a hash of public `info` — for those, std's
  `mulPublic`/`mulDoubleBasePublic` are variable-time *by design*, correct,
  and faster. This module is only for the secret side; routing public
  scalars through it buys nothing and costs speed.
- **No secrets are held.** The module allocates nothing, keeps no state and
  has no RNG; the only secret-derived values are the caller's scalar (a
  by-value parameter) and the running `q`.
  A caller can wipe its own variable but can neither see nor reach the copy the ABI makes on `mul`'s frame, so the module does it: every entry point that takes the scalar by value (`mul`, `mulBase`, `mulRistretto`, `mulRistrettoBase`) copies it into a local and `defer`s `std.crypto.secureZero` on that copy (`root.zig`, `:328`, `:380`, `:1884`). A painted-stack probe (`src/stackprobe_test.zig`) with its own negative and positive controls scans the dead frame after each call for the scalar and the shared secret; a PUBLIC needle driven through the same call is wiped too, because the mechanism is "argument passed by value", not "secret". The wipe adds no secret-dependent branch (the ctgrind rows are unchanged by it).

## Verification

Run `scripts/modtest ct25519` (also `-Dprofile=small`, § Build options; the stack-probe tests run in optimized modes) and the constant-time check below.

- **External anchor (class B, EXTERNAL).** RFC 8032 §7.1 TEST 1 and TEST 2
  publish Ed25519 public keys; the test re-derives each as
  `[clamp(SHA-512(sk)[0..32])]B` and requires the exact published 32 bytes.
  This is the only oracle in the module whose authority comes from outside
  the Zig tree, and it is the only one that could catch a defect *shared*
  with std — which matters precisely because the ladder here is a
  re-derivation of std's.
- **Differential vs std**, on the base point and on non-base points, over
  deterministic pseudorandom scalars (SHA-512 stream reduced mod `L`), plus
  the Ristretto255 wrapper. std is the reference for every case std is
  willing to answer.
- **Where std refuses**, an std-independent oracle is used instead:
  - `s = 0` and `s = L` are pinned to the neutral element **as a value**
    (std raises `error.IdentityElement` for both — the test pins that too,
    so the reason the module exists cannot silently evaporate);
  - a point of order exactly 8 and the identity point — inputs std rejects
    with `error.WeakPublicKey` — are checked against **repeated addition**
    for `k = 0..9`, which depends on neither ladder;
  - scalar bits 250..255 individually, and `2^256 − 1`, are checked against
    **a doubling chain** as well as against std.
- **Std-independent property**: `(a+b)·B == a·B + b·B` over the window
  seams.
- **Type-level**: all four entry points are asserted to carry no error
  union, and std's `mul` is asserted to carry one — the shape claim itself
  is a test.
- **X25519 and the field core:** RFC 7748 vectors, the iteration chains and §6.1 key pairs through every compiled backend; a differential against std over random raw and edge inputs (value and error); a field-level differential against `u512` arithmetic mod p for both asm paths (§ P6, § X25519 key generation). `test_hooks.forced` (test builds only) lets one test run hold every compiled path to std.
- **Comb and MSM:** bit-exact against the ladder and the per-term sums over every digit, carry and chunk boundary, with mutants shown to turn the differentials red (§ C3, § B9).
- **Ed25519 sign:** `signEd25519` is held to std's `KeyPair.sign` byte for byte on 4000 random seeds, messages of 0-299 bytes and alternating `null` / random noise, each result also checked by std's `verifyStrict`, plus RFC 8032 §7.1 TEST 1 and the `KeyMismatch` refusal of a key pair whose two public halves disagree (`root.zig`, tests "signEd25519 …"). Constant time: ctgrind target `sign` (the whole secret key, seed and embedded public half, tainted after an untainted key generation) reads 0 in-file contexts on the native and the `x86_64` build. Its two branches are on public values, each computed branch-free and declassified: the `KeyMismatch` verdict (two copies of the public key) and the `R = O` verdict (probability 2^-252, std's `IdentityElement`; `R` is the returned signature's public half). With a plain `std.mem.eql` on `R` the row read 1 in-file context at that line, and `mls`'s rows, which taint a whole key pair, read 1 at the `KeyMismatch` compare (the positive controls, 2026-11-25).
- **Ed25519 verify and encode:** `verifyEd25519Strict` is held to std's `verifyStrict` for the verdict AND the error value over valid, mutated, torsion and non-canonical inputs, including a forged signature with `R` the identity or `(0,-1)` (`root.zig`, `:3072`) and the RFC 8032 §7.1 vectors (`:3008`); `mulBaseEncode` / `mulBaseEncode2` against the window ladder (`:2880`, `:2942`).
- **Fuzz:** `CT25519_FUZZ` runs the deterministic driver (`src/fuzz_test.zig`) over `verifyEd25519Strict` against std's `verifyStrict` (valid signatures, bit flips in signature / key / message, `S + L`, small-order and non-canonical `R` / `A`, mixed-order points, random bytes) and `X25519.scalarmult` / `recoverPublicKey` against std for random and low-order `u`; every reach label is hit.
- **Stack probes:** `src/stackprobe_test.zig` (every secret-scalar entry point: no scalar or shared-secret image in the dead stack afterwards, with negative and positive controls, and since 2026-11-23 the residue rule `testkit.stackprobe.residueOf` over each snapshot, which found the comb's frames below `fastBaseMul`'s state wipe while `mul`/`mulBase` burned nothing; every secret-scalar primitive now burns, `burn.mul_burn` / `burn.base_burn`; optimized modes only) and `src/stackprobe2_test.zig` (X25519 key generation, and the figures of README *Stack use*: Straus tables, burn sizes, the four entry points run in a 64 KiB thread).
- **Gaps the mutation runs closed (now tests):** the portable 4-bit comb, which a BMI2 host never reaches through `mulBase`, is called directly by `expectCombMatchesLadder`; `mul121665` drops a carry only when a limb's low product word is `2^64−1` over a large limb below it (probability about 2^-47 for random limbs), so a constructed-limb test drives it; `combRecode5`'s digit range `[-16, 15]` is value-invisible (`+16` and `-16` plus a carry give the same point), so a direct range-and-reconstruction test pins it; `wipeState` zeroes the whole state. Not killable in the ReleaseSafe killer: dropping `mul`'s `secureZero` of its scalar copy (the stack probe runs in optimized modes only). Unreached on non-BMI2 targets: `verifyTailStd` and the non-fast `mulBaseEncode2` branch (the host takes the 4×64 paths).
- **Audit:** the card's `**Audit:**` line is the current score, cumulative over the last whole-module mutation run and the delta runs after it.

### Constant-time check (ctgrind-style, valgrind memcheck)

Reasoning is not the evidence here; the harness is, and
it is a **committed program**, not a code block a reader has to retype:
[`src/ctgrind_harness.zig`](src/ctgrind_harness.zig), driven by
[`../../scripts/checks/ctgrind.sh`](../../scripts/checks/ctgrind.sh). It
marks a runtime (not comptime-folded) scalar uninitialised with valgrind's
client request, forces a volatile reload so the optimizer cannot keep a
defined register copy from before the taint, drives it through either
`mulRistrettoBase` (`--target ct25519`, what all of `voprf`'s secret-scalar
call sites reduce to) or `std.crypto.ecc.Ristretto255.mul`
(`--target std` — the function this module replaces, run as the negative
control), and finally prints the result through `std.debug.print`
(deliberately not constant-time) as a propagation witness. Run it:

```sh
scripts/checks/ctgrind.sh ct25519
```

**Full control table** for the two original targets, ReleaseFast, x86_64 (`in-file` = memcheck error CONTEXTS, not error count, whose
stack includes the named file — the number the "constant-time" claim is
actually about; `total` includes the harness's own `std.debug.print`, which
is not constant-time by design — see "propagation witness" above):

| target | `-fvalgrind` | scalar tainted | total contexts | contexts in target's own code | exit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ct25519` (`mulRistrettoBase`) | yes | **yes** | 2 | **0** in `root.zig` | 99 |
| `ct25519` | yes | no | 0 | 0 | 0 *(control)* |
| `ct25519` | **no** | yes | 0 | 0 | 0 *(trap)* |
| `std` (`Ristretto255.mul`) | yes | **yes** | 3 | **1** in `edwards25519.zig` | 99 |
| `std` | yes | no | 0 | 0 | 0 *(control)* |
| `std` | **no** | yes | 0 | 0 | 0 *(trap)* |

Reading each row:

- **Row 1 is the claim**, measured: tainting the scalar and driving it
  through this module's own `mul` produces **zero** memcheck contexts
  anywhere in `root.zig`. The 2 total contexts are both inside the harness's
  `std.debug.print` (`Io.Writer.printHex`) — proof the taint reached the
  *output*, so "zero in `root.zig`" means "no branch found", not "taint
  never arrived here".
- **Row 2 is the paired negative control** the first row is meaningless
  without: with the identical binary and the identical code path, an
  *untainted* scalar reports zero everywhere, including the print. If row 1
  read 2/0 regardless of whether the scalar was tainted, that would mean the
  print always trips memcheck for some unrelated reason — it does not.
- **Row 3 is the trap**, reproduced deliberately: built *without*
  `-fvalgrind`, `std.valgrind.doClientRequest`'s
  `if (!builtin.valgrind_support) return default;` makes `MAKE_MEM_UNDEFINED`
  silently do nothing, so even a genuinely tainted scalar reports 0/0 — a
  clean run that measured nothing, not evidence of anything.
- **Rows 4-6 are the actual point of the exercise**: the *same* harness, the
  *same* tainted scalar, routed through `std.crypto.ecc.Ristretto255.mul`
  instead — the function `ct25519` exists to replace. Row 4 reports a real
  context **inside `edwards25519.zig`**, at exactly the line this module's
  doc comments name: `pcMul16`'s `try q.rejectIdentity()`
  (`edwards25519.zig`, `if (p.x.isZero()) return error.IdentityElement;`
  in `rejectIdentity` itself). That the *same* harness, the *same* scalar,
  the *same* build flags produce a real hit on std and none on this module
  is what makes row 1's zero mean "this module removed the leak", not
  "this harness cannot see leaks". Rows 5-6 are std's own paired control and
  trap, included for symmetry — they read exactly like ct25519's.

**Reproduce the claim row directly:**

```sh
scripts/lib/capped zig build-exe modules/ct25519/src/ctgrind_harness.zig \
    -OReleaseFast -fno-strip -fvalgrind -femit-bin=/tmp/ct25519_ctgrind
valgrind --tool=memcheck --error-exitcode=99 /tmp/ct25519_ctgrind ct25519 yes
```

**Two traps that make this harness silently meaningless — both are now
rows in the table above rather than assumed.**

1. **`-fvalgrind` is mandatory outside Debug** (table rows 3, 6). Without it
   every client request compiles to nothing and the harness reports
   `0 errors` *unconditionally*, tainted or not.
2. **The volatile reload is mandatory** (`reloadVolatile` in the harness).
   Without it the optimizer can keep a *defined* register copy of the scalar
   from the hash that produced it, and the ladder never reads the memory
   that was marked — same false clean, and nothing in the table above would
   catch it, since it looks identical to a genuinely clean run.
3. Run it at **ReleaseFast**, not Debug or ReleaseSafe. There, Zig's own
   integer-overflow safety checks inside `std.crypto.25519.field`
   (`Fe.mul`/`sq`/`add`/`sub`/`_carry128`) are themselves conditional jumps
   on the tainted limbs and flood the report. **Measured**: the identical
   `ct25519`/tainted/`-fvalgrind` build at `-OReleaseSafe` reports
   **89 956 errors from 1000 contexts** — 1000 being valgrind's own default
   `--error-limit` cutoff ("More than 1000 different errors detected. I'm
   not reporting any more."), i.e. the true count is capped, not exactly
   1000. Their outcome is invariant — the limbs are masked to 51 bits and
   cannot overflow — so they are not a leak, but they bury the signal
   completely, which is why the claim above is stated for ReleaseFast only.

**Teeth.** Injecting
`var z: u8 = 0; for (s) |b| z |= b; if (z == 0) return identityElement;` at
the top of `mul` and re-running `scripts/checks/ctgrind.sh ct25519` moves row 1 from
`2 total / 0 in-file` to **`3 total / 1 in root.zig`, exit 99** — the harness
catches the exact defect class the module exists to prevent. Reverted;
`cmp` against a pre-mutation copy confirmed byte-identical, `git diff
--stat` empty.

**Always re-run the positive control after changing the harness.** A ctgrind
run that reports nothing is indistinguishable from a ctgrind run that is not
wired up — which is why the table above keeps both controls next to the
claim instead of stating the claim alone.

**What stops the harness rotting.** `zig build check-ctgrind` compiles it
(with `-fvalgrind`, so the client-request bodies are actually analysed) and
is part of `zig build test`; it runs no valgrind, so the gate neither needs
that tool installed nor pays for a memcheck run. `scripts/checks/ctgrind.sh --check`
re-measures and compares against `scripts/checks/ctgrind-expected.tsv`, asserting
that every control and trap row is 0 and that this table's in-file counts are
unchanged. Neither compares the prose above against either — see
`scripts/README.md` § Constant-time harnesses for exactly what each does and
does not catch.

### What the in-suite tests provably cannot catch

A secret-dependent branch that does not change any output byte is invisible
to every test in this file, by construction. Injecting

```zig
var z: u8 = 0;
for (s) |b| z |= b;
if (z == 0) return Edwards25519.identityElement;   // exactly the defect the module exists to prevent
```

into `mul` leaves `zig build test-ct25519` **green (exit 0)** — the output is
byte-identical on every input — while `scripts/checks/ctgrind.sh ct25519` catches it
(**exit 99**, 1 context in `root.zig`, up from 0 — see "Teeth" above for the exact command and revert). That asymmetry is the
reason the harness is documented here rather than treated as optional:
**for this module the valgrind run is not a nicety, it is the only oracle
for the property the module is named after.** Re-run it after any change to
`mul`, `pcSelect`, `precompute`, or the comb (`combRecode`, `combSelect`,
`combMulBase`, the table). The table above covers the two original targets; the
`comb`, `ladderbase`, `ladder`, `msm` and `x25519` targets and their positive controls are in the sections of those features (§ C3, § B9, § X25519 key generation, § P6).

## P7 — X25519 shared secret: ladder order and ADX squaring

**Why.** `tls13`'s bench (vs OpenSSL 3.5.5) had `cli_x25519` at 1.16×, the
one row keeping it off P2; the cause was this module's shared-secret ladder,
1.21× OpenSSL's `x25519-x86_64` on the same 4×64 radix.

**What changed.**
1. The ladder step's field operations reordered so independent ones are
   adjacent (D, B, A, C; DA ∥ CB; BB ∥ AA; ...), OpenSSL's
   `x25519_scalar_mulx` order (`crypto/ec/curve25519.c`): the out-of-order
   core overlaps the multiply chains that the dependent order serialised.
2. On the ADX path the squaring uses two interleaved carry chains
   (`sq_adx`, ported from OpenSSL's `x25519_fe64_sqr`, Apache-2.0, `NOTICE`)
   instead of the single-chain `sq_mulx`.
3. Tried and dropped: `cswap` as scalar asm (to avoid LLVM's 32-byte vector
   loads of limbs just stored as 8-byte words) — 5 % SLOWER than the
   vectorised Zig `cswap` once the order was fixed; JCC-erratum padding
   (`-Djcc-safe`) — no change in the ratio. (The scalar-asm `cswap` is reversed on Zig 0.17.1: see P9.)

Correctness: RFC 7748 vectors and the field differential against std in Debug, ReleaseFast and an `x86_64_v3` (MULX-only) build; the ctgrind rows are unchanged in count.

## P8 — Edwards25519 on the 4×64 field: comb, verify

On the 4×64 field the field multiplication was not the lever (std's `Fe` mul and `fe64` mul take the same time, latency-bound); the point formulas were:


- **Comb** (`EdOps.combMulBase`): ref10's shape but with signed radix-32 digits — 52 digits, 26 rows × 16 entries (26 × 16 entries of 96 bytes = 39 936 bytes, no `2^256·B` carry term: the top digit cannot carry), 52 mixed additions + 5 doublings instead of 65 additions + 4; the select is a `@Vector(4,u64)` masked blend (the scalar version of 16 entries cost more than the saved additions) and the sign is applied in the vector domain. Table entries affine `(y+x, y−x, 2d·xy)` (96 B, batch-inverted at comptime), mixed addition 7M instead of std's 9M, three coordinates per `cMov` select instead of four, sign by swapping y+x/y−x and negating 2d·xy. Same digit recoding, row order, 256-bit carry term as the std-field comb (which stays as the fallback where there is no MULX or the backend is not LLVM). Constant time: `selectComb`'s masks go through an empty-asm barrier (`opaque_mask`) — without it LLVM turned the sign handling into a branch on the secret digit (ctgrind: 2 in-file contexts; with the barrier: 0).
- **Verify** (`verifyEd25519Strict`): std's order of checks (S < L, A decodes via std's lenient decoder, A not identity, R canonical, R decodes, R not identity, A not of small order = x of 4A ≠ 0, cofactorless equation). `[S]B − [h]A` by wNAF (w=8 over a 64-entry odd-multiple affine table for B, w=5 over 8 projective entries for A), doublings without `t` where no addition follows. R is never decoded on the success path: Q is encoded (one inversion) and compared with R's bytes; on any mismatch the error std would have given is computed (`rError`). Differentially tested against std for the error value, not just accept/reject.
- **Encode**: `mulBaseEncode` avoids std's `toBytes` inversion (4.5 µs → 3.2 µs on `fe64`); `mulBaseEncode2` shares one inversion between two points.

Tried and not worth it: wiping the `fe64.State` with vector stores instead of `secureZero` (no change). The Ed25519 sign and verify rows of `bench-tls13` carry the figures against aws-lc-rs.

## P9 — X25519 ladder: asm `cswap`, fused add/sub

**Why.** `tls13`'s fastest-implementation column had `cli_x25519` over the 1.25 the P1 row allows against aws-lc-rs 1.18.0 (s2n-bignum).

**Measured first.** `perf annotate` of `bench-ct25519 x25519`: the hottest instruction of the ladder was
`vmovdqu` in `cswap` — LLVM vectorised the Zig loop into 32-byte loads of limbs the asm blocks had just written as
8-byte stores, and a load wider than the stores it reads is not store-forwarded.

**What changed.**
1. `fe64.cswap` on the asm path is asm (`cswap_asm`: 64-bit loads, `t = m & (x ^ y)`, 64-bit stores) — the
   opposite of P7's finding on Zig 0.17.0, where the scalar asm swap measured slower; on 0.17.1 it is
   faster, so the toolchain moved the balance.
2. `addsub_asm`: the three sum/difference pairs of a step taken from the same two inputs (C/D from x3,z3; A/B
   from x2,z2; DA±CB) are one block each, the first input loaded once — five add/sub blocks a step instead
   of eight.
Constant time unchanged in kind: straight-line, a mask, no branch; ctgrind rows for ct25519 (ct25519, comb,
ladderbase, ladder, msm, x25519) unchanged in count, digests re-pinned.

Correctness: the field differential and RFC 7748 vectors over every backend (§ Verification).

## P10 — X25519 ladder: what the profile says, and four changes measured and not kept

`cli_x25519` against aws-lc-rs (s2n-bignum) stays at 1.26× in the `tls13` bench (P1 bound 1.25; ours 29.9 µs, aws-lc-rs
23.8 µs, spread 1 %). `perf annotate` of `bench-ct25519 x25519`: 89 % of the cycles are the 255-step loop, 952
instructions a step at IPC ≈ 2.7 (no single hot instruction; the profile is flat), 9.5 % the inversion chain
(265 dependent squarings and multiplications, ≈ 36 cycles each). A step is bound by the carry-flag and
multiply ports (≈ 160 `mulx`, several hundred `adc`/`sbb`/`adcx`/`adox`, which run on two ports), not by one
instruction, and the asm blocks execute almost in program order (a block of ≈ 90 micro-ops fills the scheduler).
Measured in the shield, ABAB, with the cycle ratio against libsodium as the metric (spread ≤ 0.3 %; the ns column
moves ± 3 % between invocations, the ratio does not): baseline 0.785–0.789.

| change | cycle ratio | kept |
|---|---|---|
| `E = AA − BB`, `a24·E` and `AA + a24·E` in one block (`E` stays in registers, the product is added as five words and folded once): 29 instructions a step fewer | 0.795, 0.798 | no (slower: the block is one long dependent chain) |
| the state addressed through two base registers so that the 15 ladder slots all take an 8-bit displacement (code ≈ 20 % shorter) | 0.789, 0.788 | no (no gain) |
| ladder order with the critical chain `DA, CB → DA±CB → (DA−CB)² → z3` first | 0.822, 0.826 | no (+4.5 %) |
| the same, `(DA−CB)²` and `(DA+CB)²` right after `DA±CB`, `AA`/`BB` after them | 0.841, 0.849 | no (+8 %) |
| squares first, then the products, `x2` and `E` before `DA±CB` | 0.795, 0.796 | no (equal) |

The order of `P7` (OpenSSL's) is a local optimum: moving a consumer next to its producer costs 4–8 %. What would
still pay is fusing the product blocks (interleaving two multiplications' `mulx` rows in one block, impossible in 15
registers) or lazy five-word `mul_5`-style operands for `DA ± CB` (s2n-bignum's way, two folds a step), a new field
core rather than a tuning pass.

## Performance — `bench-ct25519`

`zig build bench-ct25519` (`tools/bench.zig` driving `tools/c_bench/foreign_bench.c`) is the comparative benchmark behind the card's `**Performance:**` line, which carries the figures and is authoritative. **Reference: libsodium 1.0.18** (system `libsodium.so.23`) as a stand-in: the scope's reference, curve25519-dalek 5.0, is a Rust crate that is not measured here. The X25519 rows also run OpenSSL 3.5.5 (`libcrypto.so.3`, the `x25519-x86_64` MULX/ADX assembly), the faster of the two there and the card's `fastest`. The foreign side is built with `zig cc -O3 -march=native`.

Method: each side doubles its batch until it takes over 100 ms and keeps the best of five; per workload the sides alternate for `BENCH_ROUNDS` rounds and each keeps its best; ratio = ours/theirs by user-mode cycles; spread = (worst round − best round) / best round per side, printed per row (a row measured under host load is to be repeated). Before timing, an interop check: every foreign output — both X25519s from both libraries, the Edwards and Ristretto base multiples — must equal ours byte for byte.

Workloads, encoded output included on both sides: `x25519` = `X25519.scalarmultInto` vs `crypto_scalarmult` / OpenSSL `EVP_PKEY_derive` (peer set once); `x25519_pub` = `X25519.recoverPublicKeyInto` vs `crypto_scalarmult_base` / OpenSSL raw-key import + `get_raw_public_key`; `ed_base` = `mulBase(s).toBytes()` vs `crypto_scalarmult_ed25519_base_noclamp`; `rist_base` = `mulRistrettoBase(s).toBytes()` vs `crypto_scalarmult_ristretto255_base`. Not compared: the variable-base Edwards/Ristretto `mul` — libsodium's `crypto_scalarmult_ed25519_noclamp` adds a prime-order-subgroup check (a second scalar multiplication) that `mul` does not do.

`CT25519_BENCH=1 scripts/modtest ct25519 -Doptimize=ReleaseFast` (`src/bench.zig`) re-runs the in-module pairs (comb against ladder, `recoverPublicKey` against std, the MSM against the per-term sum, the X25519 ladder against std).

## Build options

Consumer build options (CONVENTIONS §4.2), added at the router-tool consumer's request:

| option | values | default | `-Dprofile=small` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ct25519-base-comb` | `true` / `false` | `true` (graded) | `false` |

- **`false`:** `mulBase`, `mulRistrettoBase` and `X25519.recoverPublicKey` run on `mul`'s window ladder over `base_pc` instead
  of the fixed-base comb (`baseMul`, src/root.zig). Same result for every 256-bit `s` — the ladder is the reference the comb is
  differentially tested against.
- **What it buys:** the 43 008-byte `comb_table` and its select/recode code. A probe doing one X25519 keygen (ReleaseSmall,
  x86_64-musl, stripped): **57 696 → 17 176 B**.
- **What it costs:** keygen/sign speed. bench (ReleaseFast, this machine): X25519 public key 22.8 → 55.7 µs (2.4×; std's is
  ~50 µs), Edwards/ristretto base point 21.5 → 56 µs. DH (`X25519.scalarmult`) unchanged. Under `.small` the bench's `comb_*` rows
  measure the ladder (the label names the entry point, not the algorithm).
- **Constant time:** `CTGRIND_ZIG_ARGS="-Dprofile=small" scripts/checks/ctgrind.sh ct25519`: `comb` and `x25519`
  rows 0 in-file contexts, controls 0, traps 0. The expected table pins the default build only.
- **Tested:** `scripts/modtest ct25519 -Dprofile=small` in Debug, ReleaseSafe and ReleaseFast (stackprobe runs in ReleaseFast:
  the ladder's stack stays within `burn.x25519_base_burn`); `sealedbox -Dprofile=small`.

## What is deliberately not done

- **A fused X25519 ladder step** — one asm block per step with `x2, z2, x3, z3` kept in registers and the add/sub pairs merged is where the published x86-64 ladders get their remaining margin. Not planned: it trades about 200 lines of reviewable asm per operation for one ~1 000-line block, for an estimated further 10–25 %.
- **Sizing the Straus tables by `points.len`.** The chunk (`msm_chunk = 8`) is a stack bound, not a tuning knob; more terms run in further passes (README *Stack use*).
- **A constant-time safegcd (Bernstein–Yang) inverse in place of the Fermat chain** at the end of the ladder (about 10 % of a ladder). Not built: the shared-secret rows reached their target without it (§ P7).
- **Validating the input point, or rejecting an identity result.** `mul` and its siblings take no `WeakPublicKey` check and return the neutral element as a value; the caller validates the point (§ Threat model / limits).
- **Variable-time MSM, hash-to-curve, Elligator and the point types themselves** — public-data operations `std` provides, outside this module's secret-scalar scope (§ Compared with).

## Backlog / deferred

- **A prepared Ed25519 signer (2026-11-25).** `signEd25519` expands the seed (one SHA-512) on every call, as std does. `tls13`'s `certverify.Ed25519Signer` keeps the clamped scalar and the nonce prefix from load time and checks the public half once, over its own copy of the RFC 8032 body (`certverify.signCore`, the same comb calls). One prepared type here (expand + check at init, wipe at deinit) would serve both; then `tls13` calls it and its copy goes. Not done in the change that added `signEd25519`: it touches `tls13`'s ctgrind rows and API, a separate step.
- **aarch64 field core for the X25519 shared secret and the comb:** the field core is x86-64 MULX/ADX inline assembly and other targets run `std`'s ladder unchanged, so an ARM server gets none of the win. Effort: medium (a 4×64 core with `umulh`, reusing the field differential of § P6). Fits CONVENTIONS §2 (inline asm is native Zig).

## Anchoring

**Anchor grade:** class B · oracle EXTERNAL

- **Class B** — published cryptographic or algorithmic construction with published vectors.
- **Oracle EXTERNAL** — published vectors, goldens captured from a foreign implementation, or a test run against a live foreign peer.

**What the tests actually contain.** RFC 8032 §7.1 TEST 1/2 public keys re-derived byte-exact; bit-exact vs std.crypto.ecc.Edwards25519.mul/Ristretto255.mul
